## Setup

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. $\mathcal N(0,1)$. The density of interest is $f(0)$, estimated by

$$
\hat f_K(x)=\frac{1}{nh}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{X_i-x}{h}\right).
$$

We compare the *uniform* and *Epanechnikov* kernels:

$$
\begin{aligned}
K_U(u)&=\mathbf 1\{-1/2<u\leq 1/2\},\\
K_E(u)&=\frac{3}{4\sqrt 5}\left(1-\frac{u^2}{5}\right)\mathbf 1\{|u|\leq\sqrt5\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the standard normal density, $f(0)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}$ and $f^{(2)}(0)=-f(0)$. The kernel constants and AMSE-optimal bandwidth are

$$
\begin{array}{c|cc}
K&\mu_2(K)&R(K)\\\hline
\text{Uniform}&1/12&1\\
\text{Epanechnikov}&1&3/(5\sqrt{5})
\end{array}
$$

$$
h_{\mathrm{opt},K}=\left\{\frac{f(0)R(K)}{[f^{(2)}(0)]^2\mu_2(K)^2}\right\}^{1/5}n^{-1/5}.
$$

## Density plots for one sample ($n=200$)

The two plots below use the same normal sample. Each panel has one kernel estimate (solid) and the true $\mathcal N(0,1)$ density (dashed black). The horizontal and vertical scales are the same across panels.

For the last question in (b), change `bandwidth_factor` from `1` to `0.5` or `2`, then re-run this same code cell. This changes the bandwidths in both panels without adding a separate sensitivity plot. The optimal bandwidth is computed for $x=0$, even though we display the entire density curve.

```{webr}
bandwidth_factor <- 1  # Try 0.5 or 2 by changing this line.

set.seed(123)

K_U <- function(u) as.numeric(u > -0.5 & u <= 0.5)
K_E <- function(u) {
  value <- 3 / (4 * sqrt(5)) * (1 - u^2 / 5)
  value[abs(u) > sqrt(5)] <- 0
  pmax(value, 0)
}

f0 <- dnorm(0)
fpp0 <- -f0
mu2 <- c(Uniform = 1/12, Epanechnikov = 1)
RK <- c(Uniform = 1, Epanechnikov = 3/(5*sqrt(5)))

h_opt <- function(n, kernel_name) {
  unname((f0 * RK[kernel_name] /
            (n * fpp0^2 * mu2[kernel_name]^2))^(1/5))
}

kde <- function(grid, data, bandwidth, kernel) {
  vapply(grid, function(x) mean(kernel((data - x) / bandwidth)) /
           bandwidth, numeric(1))
}

n_plot <- 200
X <- rnorm(n_plot)

hU <- bandwidth_factor * h_opt(n_plot, "Uniform")
hE <- bandwidth_factor * h_opt(n_plot, "Epanechnikov")
grid <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 401)
truth <- dnorm(grid)
fitU <- kde(grid, X, hU, K_U)
fitE <- kde(grid, X, hE, K_E)

# Two panels: Uniform (left), Epanechnikov (right).
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 0.8))
y_lim <- range(c(0, truth, fitU, fitE))

plot(grid, truth, type = "l", lty = 2, col = "black", lwd = 2,
     ylim = y_lim, xlab = "x", ylab = "Density",
     main = "Uniform kernel")
lines(grid, fitU, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
abline(v = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey60")
legend("topright", c("True", "KDE"),
       col = c("black", "steelblue"), lty = c(2, 1), lwd = 2,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.77)

plot(grid, truth, type = "l", lty = 2, col = "black", lwd = 2,
     ylim = y_lim, xlab = "x", ylab = "Density",
     main = "Epanechnikov kernel")
lines(grid, fitE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
abline(v = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey60")
legend("topright", c("True", "KDE"),
       col = c("black", "firebrick"), lty = c(2, 1), lwd = 2,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.77)
par(old_par)
```

The uniform KDE is a step function, while the Epanechnikov KDE is continuous. Halving a bandwidth generally makes the estimate more irregular; doubling it produces stronger smoothing, with a possible increase in bias.

## Minimized AMSE

At the optimum, the asymptotic variance is four times the squared leading bias. Therefore,

$$
\mathrm{AMSE}_K(h_{\mathrm{opt},K};0)
=\frac54 h_{\mathrm{opt},K}^4[f^{(2)}(0)\mu_2(K)]^2.
$$

Substituting the normal density and the kernel constants gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{AMSE}_U(h_{\mathrm{opt},U};0)&\simeq 0.153578\,n^{-4/5},\\
\mathrm{AMSE}_E(h_{\mathrm{opt},E};0)&\simeq 0.144856\,n^{-4/5},\\
\frac{\mathrm{AMSE}_E(h_{\mathrm{opt},E};0)}
{\mathrm{AMSE}_U(h_{\mathrm{opt},U};0)}&\simeq 0.9432.
\end{aligned}
$$

The leading pointwise MSE favors Epanechnikov by about $5.7\%$.

## Monte Carlo MSE comparison ($n=2000$, $B=5000$)

For each replication, draw one standard normal sample of size $n=2000$. Each kernel gets its own pointwise AMSE-optimal bandwidth. The table reports Monte Carlo MSE, and the MSE ratio is compared with the theoretical prediction.

```{webr}
set.seed(123)

K_U <- function(u) as.numeric(u > -0.5 & u <= 0.5)
K_E <- function(u) {
  value <- 3 / (4 * sqrt(5)) * (1 - u^2 / 5)
  value[abs(u) > sqrt(5)] <- 0
  pmax(value, 0)
}
f0 <- dnorm(0)
fpp0 <- -f0
mu2 <- c(Uniform = 1/12, Epanechnikov = 1)
RK <- c(Uniform = 1, Epanechnikov = 3/(5*sqrt(5)))
h_opt <- function(n, kernel_name) {
  unname((f0 * RK[kernel_name] /
            (n * fpp0^2 * mu2[kernel_name]^2))^(1/5))
}

n <- 2000
B <- 5000
h <- c(Uniform = h_opt(n, "Uniform"),
       Epanechnikov = h_opt(n, "Epanechnikov"))

est <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = B, ncol = 2,
              dimnames = list(NULL, names(h)))
for (rep in seq_len(B)) {
  X <- rnorm(n)  # One sample per replication, shared by both kernels.
  est[rep, "Uniform"] <- mean(K_U(X / h["Uniform"])) / h["Uniform"]
  est[rep, "Epanechnikov"] <-
    mean(K_E(X / h["Epanechnikov"])) / h["Epanechnikov"]
}

mc_mse <- colMeans((est - f0)^2)

result <- data.frame(
  Kernel = names(h),
  MC_MSE = unname(mc_mse)
)
cat("Monte Carlo summary:\n")
print(result, row.names = FALSE, digits = 5)
cat(sprintf("Monte Carlo MSE E/U ratio = %.4f\n",
            unname(mc_mse["Epanechnikov"] / mc_mse["Uniform"])))
```

The Monte Carlo MSE is expected to be smaller under Epanechnikov, with a reduction comparable to the theoretical prediction.

## Normal approximation

Consider the following conventional standardized statistic:

$$
Z_{n,E}=\frac{\sqrt{nh_{\mathrm{opt},E}}\{\hat f_E(0)-f(0)\}}
{\sqrt{f(0)R(K_E)}}.
$$

At the AMSE-optimal bandwidth, its standardized bias is $-1/2$; thus $Z_{n,E}$ is asymptotically $\mathcal N(-1/2,1)$, **not** $\mathcal N(0,1)$.

Run the Monte Carlo code in the previous section before running the following cell, which uses the same replications.

```{webr}
hE <- unname(h["Epanechnikov"])
RE <- unname(RK["Epanechnikov"])
bE <- 0.5 * hE^2 * fpp0 * mu2["Epanechnikov"]
seE <- sqrt(f0 * RE / (n * hE))
Z_E <- (est[, "Epanechnikov"] - f0) / seE
predicted_center <- unname(bE / seE)

cat(sprintf("Monte Carlo mean of Z = %.4f\n",
            mean(Z_E)))

hist(Z_E, breaks = 35, freq = FALSE, col = "grey85",
     border = "white", main = "Epanechnikov",
     xlab = "Z_n,E", ylab = "Density")
curve(dnorm(x, mean = 0, sd = 1), add = TRUE,
      col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
curve(dnorm(x, mean = predicted_center, sd = 1), add = TRUE,
      col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = mean(Z_E), lty = 3, col = "black", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("N(0,1)", "N(-1/2,1)", "Monte Carlo mean"),
       col = c("firebrick", "steelblue", "black"),
       lty = c(1, 2, 3), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

The empirical distribution of $Z_{n,E}$ is approximately normal, but it is centered around the standardized asymptotic bias rather than zero. Consequently, conventional confidence intervals that ignore this bias may suffer from coverage distortion.
